newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir ends polling, looks to democracy.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir ends polling, looks to democracy.

text.p: Scattered gunfire punctuated the last day of voting in local polls in India's Jammu and Kashmir state on Monday but there were no reported deaths as the region prepared for the return of democracy.
About 56 percent of eligible voters turned out on the fourth and final day of balloting for the state assembly, which was dissolved in 1990 after a separatist revolt erupted.
The turnout was described as "quite satisfactory" by an official in the state's summer capital Srinagar shortly after polling ended at 5 p.m. (1130 GMT).

Officials had said an estimated 300,000 people in the mountainous Doda district, 250 km (150 miles) south of Srinagar, were eligible to vote for 45 candidates in the polls to six of the state's 87 assembly seats.
Some 22,000 paramilitary troops guarded the polls.
Many of the guerrilla groups fighting either for independence or merger with Islamic Pakistan have hide-outs in Doda's bleak terrain and officials had feared voters would be the target of attacks.
Security forces exchanged fire with militants in four incidents during the day. Voting was disrupted for about half an hour in two cases, but was soon back on track, officials said.
The streets of Srinagar were mostly deserted and shops were shut as residents observed a strike called by the separatist All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, which opposes the polls.
In the downtown Maisooma area, some opponents of the polls threw stones at security forces, authorities said.
With the polling for the first assembly elections since 1987 now complete, officials began to prepare for the new government, expected to take power by early next week.

"I am sanguine that the new government will strive its utmost to meet your expectations and aspirations," governor K.V. Krishna Rao, a retired general, said in an address on state-run Doordarshan television.

"They have a challenging task in furthering peace and preventing another proxy war, continuing reconstruction and rehabilitation, tackling the unemployment problem and reviving the state's economy," he said.
India accuses Pakistan of arming and funding Moslem separatists, charges which Islamabad has always denied.
Voters said they hoped for peace after the elections.
"It will ease pressure on us from pro-government and separatist militants. We want to live in peace. That's our priority," Mohammed Aslam Khan, 38, told Reuters.
The federal government in New Delhi has ruled the state directly since 1990, when the state assembly was dissolved after the separatist revolt flared.
Police and hospitals say more than 20,000 people have since died in insurgency-related violence.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left government in New Delhi hopes the elections will pave the way for the return of normalcy to the rugged Himalayan region.
The polls were staggered in four phases spread over a month to permit the movement of thousands of security forces and polling staff.
At least 21 people, mostly political activists, have been killed in election-related violence.
Farooq Abdullah, the chief of the state's largest party, the National Conference, escaped two grenade attacks. He was tipped to become chief minister.
Vote counting was set to start on Tuesday, and initial trends were expected by Wednesday, officials said.
